title.en: Why species diversity matters to an ecosystem

body.en: Ecologists have long believed that communities with more species tend to be more stable than those with fewer species; a stable community should not show too much variation in productivity from year to year, should be resistant or resilient to occasional disturbances, and should be resistant to invasions by alien species. David Tilman's long-term ecosystem experiments using outdoor plots found that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass. He also showed that increased diversity contributed to higher productivity. Stanford ecologist Paul Ehrlich explained the importance of each species with the rivet popper hypothesis: in an airplane (the ecosystem) all parts are joined together by thousands of rivets (species). If every passenger pops a rivet to take home (causing a species to become extinct), it may not affect flight safety initially, but as more rivets are removed the plane becomes dangerously weak. Which rivet is removed also matters: loss of rivets on the wings (key species that drive major ecosystem functions) is obviously more serious than loss of a few rivets on the seats or windows inside the plane.

points.en: Tilman: more species → less year-to-year variation in biomass, higher productivity
Wing rivets = key species driving major functions

narration.en: Tilman's experiments showed that plots with more species have steadier and higher productivity. Paul Ehrlich's rivet popper hypothesis compares species to the rivets of an aeroplane: losing a few may not matter, but losing many, or losing key species on the wings, can bring it down.
narration.kn: ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಪ್ರಭೇದಗಳಿರುವ ಕ್ಷೇತ್ರಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಉತ್ಪಾದಕತೆ ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಸ್ಥಿರ ಮತ್ತು ಅಧಿಕ ಎಂದು ಟಿಲ್ಮನ್ ಪ್ರಯೋಗಗಳು ತೋರಿಸಿದವು. ಪಾಲ್ ಎರ್ಲಿಕ್‌ರ ರಿವೆಟ್ ಪಾಪರ್ ಪರಿಕಲ್ಪನೆ ಪ್ರಭೇದಗಳನ್ನು ವಿಮಾನದ ರಿವೆಟ್‌ಗಳಿಗೆ ಹೋಲಿಸುತ್ತದೆ: ಕೆಲವು ಹೋದರೆ ತೊಂದರೆಯಿಲ್ಲ, ಆದರೆ ಹಲವು ಅಥವಾ ರೆಕ್ಕೆಯ ಪ್ರಮುಖ ಪ್ರಭೇದಗಳು ಹೋದರೆ ವ್ಯವಸ್ಥೆ ಕುಸಿಯುತ್ತದೆ.

title.en: Board: rivets and the Evil Quartet

say.en: Why does diversity matter? Tilman found that plots with more species varied less in biomass from year to year and were more productive.
Ehrlich’s rivet popper idea: the ecosystem is an aeroplane and the species are its rivets. Losing seat rivets may not matter at once, but losing a wing rivet, a key species, can bring the plane down.
Biodiversity is being lost through four main causes, the Evil Quartet.

text.en: The Amazon rain forest cleared for soya beans and cattle pasture
Tropical rain forests shrinking from 14 to about 6 per cent of the land
Steller's sea cow hunted to extinction
Passenger pigeons killed in huge numbers
Nile perch in Lake Victoria wiping out cichlid fish
Illegal African catfish threatening native catfishes of Indian rivers
Carrot grass (Parthenium) and Lantana spreading over native plants
Parasites dying out with the fish species they live on
A plant and its only pollinator disappearing together

explanation.en: Habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause (rain forests once covering 14 per cent of land now cover about 6 per cent). Over-exploitation wiped out Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon. Alien species like the Nile perch, Parthenium, Lantana, water hyacinth and the African catfish harm native species. Co-extinction: when a host goes extinct, its own parasites and partners go too.
explanation.kn: ಆವಾಸ ನಾಶ, ಅತಿ ಶೋಷಣೆ, ಪರಕೀಯ ಪ್ರಭೇದಗಳ ಆಕ್ರಮಣ ಮತ್ತು ಸಹ-ಅಳಿವು: ಈ ನಾಲ್ಕು ಕಾರಣಗಳು.

title.en: Loss of biodiversity and the Evil Quartet

body.en: The IUCN Red List (2004) documents the extinction of 784 species (including 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants) in the last 500 years. Recent extinctions include the dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller's sea cow (Russia) and three subspecies of tiger (Bali, Javan, Caspian). The last twenty years alone have witnessed the disappearance of 27 species. Some groups, like amphibians, appear more vulnerable. More than 15,500 species world-wide currently face the threat of extinction; 12 per cent of all bird species, 23 per cent of all mammal species, 32 per cent of all amphibian species and 31 per cent of all gymnosperm species face extinction. Current species extinction rates are estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times, and our activities are responsible: we may be in the midst of a sixth extinction. Loss of biodiversity leads to decline in plant production, lowered resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought, and increased variability in ecosystem processes such as plant productivity, water use, and pest and disease cycles. The four major causes, the "Evil Quartet": (i) habitat loss and fragmentation, the most important cause: tropical rain forests once covered more than 14 per cent of the Earth's land surface and now cover no more than 6 per cent; the Amazon rain forest, called the "lungs of the planet", is being cut and cleared for soya beans or for grasslands for beef cattle; (ii) over-exploitation: Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon were driven extinct by over-exploitation by humans; (iii) alien species invasions: the Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria in East Africa led to the extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than 200 species of cichlid fish; carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eichhornia) threaten native species; illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture threatens indigenous catfishes in our rivers; (iv) co-extinctions: when a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species obligatorily associated with it also become extinct, for example the unique parasites of a host fish, or a plant and its co-evolved pollinator.

narration.en: Extinctions today are 100 to 1,000 times faster than before humans. The four main causes, the Evil Quartet, are habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasions such as the Nile perch in Lake Victoria, and co-extinctions.

problem.en: Classify each case under the Evil Quartet: (a) water hyacinth chokes a lake in Bengaluru; (b) a forest is cut into small patches by roads and farms; (c) a fig species dies out and so does its only pollinator wasp; (d) Steller's sea cow is hunted to extinction.

steps.en: (a) Water hyacinth (Eichhornia) is an introduced species spreading aggressively: alien species invasion.
(b) Breaking a large habitat into small pieces: habitat loss and fragmentation.
(c) An obligately associated species dies with its partner: co-extinction.
(d) Killing beyond what the population can replace: over-exploitation.

answer.en: (a) alien species invasion; (b) habitat loss and fragmentation; (c) co-extinction; (d) over-exploitation.
